Jesus once made a whip. With his own hands.
And drove grown men out of the Temple.
John, chapter two.
Passover. Jerusalem. The Temple courts are packed.
Oxen. Sheep. Cages of doves. And the tables of the money changers.
The Temple tax had to be paid in one coin. The silver shekel of Tyre.
So the changers swapped your money. For a fee.
And then Jesus does something no other gospel describes.
He made a scourge of small cords.
He didn't grab a stick. He made it. Cord by cord.
And he drove them all out of the temple, the sheep, and the oxen.
He poured out the changers' money, and overthrew the tables.
But watch what he does with the doves.
Doves were the sacrifice of the poor. Mary herself offered two after Jesus was born.
He doesn't smash the cages. He tells the sellers, Take these things hence.
Make not my Father's house an house of merchandise.
The leaders demand a sign. By what authority?
His answer. Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.
Forty and six years was this temple in building, they say.
Josephus says Herod began it around twenty B C. Forty six years later lands right where John sets this scene.
But he spake of the temple of his body.
Here is the detail most people miss.
The Greek word for that whip, frahghellion, appears only once in the entire New Testament.
It comes from the Latin flagellum. A Roman scourge.
Three years later, Pilate has Jesus scourged. And Mark and Matthew use the very same word.
And his words about the temple? At his trial, they are quoted against him.
At the cross, they are shouted at him. Thou that destroyest the temple.
Forty years later, Rome burns Herod's temple to the ground.
He braided a whip for the sellers. Three years later, the whip was for him.
And the temple he promised to raise, rose on the third day.
